```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(Stat2Data)
library(broom)
library(tinytex)
library(cowplot)
data("Clothing")
```

```{r}
myClothes <- Clothing
rmCloth <- myClothes[1:59,]
```


  From the given datasets, our group selected the Clothing data set from Stat2Data, which contains a random sample of 60 observations of customers with 8 variables, collected from a large clothing retailer. This clothing retailer offers a store credit card. Our given data records the use of these cards, as well as variables on frequency, recency of latest purchase, and money spent in the past 12 and 24 months. 
Our research question is: Does holding a private-label store credit card and frequency of visits over a 24 month period affect the total dollar amount a customer spends? By understanding this, it will help the retailer find the value of their credit card program, and whether cardholder spend more, or simply visit more often. 
In investigating our data, we looked for any unusual purchase amounts within the dataset. In comparing the max, mean, and median, the range difference is significantly notable. In considering the explanatory variable, dollars spent in most recent purchase (Amount), there is an outstanding outlier with a purchase of \$1,506,000. However, the median amount spent in most recent purchase is \$70. This demonstrates a significantly skewed mean of \$25201.07. We removed this extreme observation to prevent it from disproportionately affecting our model.


```{r}
p1<- ggplot(rmCloth, aes(x = Freq12, y = Dollar12, color = factor(Card))) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "12 Month Total Spend vs. Frequency of Visits",
       x = "Number of Purchases (Last 12 Months)",
       y = "Total Dollars Spent (Last 12 Months)",
       color = "Credit Card 1=Y,0=N") +
  theme_minimal()
p2<-ggplot(rmCloth, aes(x = Freq24, y = Dollar24, color = factor(Card))) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "12 Month Total Spend vs. Frequency of Visits",
       x = "Number of Purchases (Last 24 Months)",
       y = "Total Dollars Spent (Last 24 Months)",
       color = "Credit Card 1=Y,0=N") +
  theme_minimal()
plot_grid(p1,p2)
```
In the scatter plots, it shows a clear positive, linear relationship between frequency of visits and total dollars spent over both 24 and 12. We chose to put in 12 months as well to confirm this linear trend. When grouping the data by cardholders(1) vs non cardholders, it shows a separation between the lines. Visually, cardholders appear to have higher total spending at similar frequencies compared to the ones without cards.

This visual evidences supports using a linear regression model, there is a distinct separation which supports Card being a useful categorical predictor to include alongside Freq24. The slopes of the two lines are roughly parallel, so a multiple linear regression model is a good model to fit.

```{r}
mlr.model <- lm(Dollar24 ~ Freq24 + Card, data = rmCloth)
summary(mlr.model)
mlr.conf <- augment(mlr.model, rmCloth, interval = 'confidence')

```

Our fitted multiple linear regression model is:

$$\widehat{\text{Dollar24}} = 124.70 + 57.65(\text{Freq24}) + 
289.33(\text{Card})$$


For our model, our response variable is Dollar24, the total dollar spend over the past 24 months. Our explanatory variables are Freq24, the number of purchases in the last 24 months, and Card, a binary indicator being 1 if they hold a card, 0 if not.
We chose these because it aligns the response and predictor time frame of 24 month customer activity. We chose 24 months because it gives more data of the customers past, and with this control it gives a clearer picture and prevents bias in the model.
The frequency slope, $\hat{\beta}_1(\text{Freq24})$, is interpreted as; holding store card status constant, each additional purchase over the 24 month period is associated with an estimated average increase of $57.65$ in total spending. $ p=0.000271$
The card indicator $\hat{\beta}_2(\text{Card})$ shows that for customers with the exact same frequency, holding a store credit card is associated with an average spend of 289.33 dollars over non cardholders $p=0.002179$.
The intercept $\hat{\beta}_0$ is the baseline expected spend for a non cardholder with zero visits. Every customer in the dataset visited atleast once, so Freq24 is outside the observed data range. This value is practically meaningless because it doesn't make sense in context. $p=0.126$.


```{r}
plot(mlr.model, which=1)
```
Looking at the residual vs fitted values plot, it shows random scatter centered around zero, showing that a linear model is suitable. The data represents independent customer accounts sampled. The residual spread shows some mild widening around the higher fitted values, however removing the extreme point fixed somed of the fanning compared to the raw dataset.
```{r}
plot(mlr.model, which=2)
```
The residuals shows good normality, there is some deviation at the higher and lower values, the majority of the points align with the reference line. There is a large positive residual, but it remains within acceptable limits.


To check for model improvements we looked at an interaction model to see if the rate of spending differs between card holders and non cardholders. 
```{r}
mlr.interact <- lm(Dollar24 ~ Freq24*Card, data=rmCloth)
summary(mlr.interact)
```
The interaction term Freq:Card had a p-value of .01245, this is statistically significant, but we decided to reject the interaction model and stick with our original. The goal of the model is for clear, business insights and the interaction model over complicates the interpretation, so it would be difficult to explain the true value of the credit card. Our original model is very good for interpretation, and aligns with the visual exploration, so adding complexity just to slightly increase the R square to .5366 is not practically useful. So we proceed with the original model.

Looking at the multiple R squared value of the original model, 0.4804, This tells us approximately 48.04% of the total variation in a customer's 24 month spending is explained by this model using their number of visits, and whether or not they have a store card.

There are two types of inference that we will do, first is one for the model, and second is on the specific effect of the store card. First, for the overall model we evaluate the overall F statistic. We produced an F statistic of 25.88 on 2 and 56 df, with a pvalue of 1.095e-08. This p value is extremely small below the 0.05 significance level, we reject the null hypothesis that all slope coefficients are zero. We have very strong evidence that at least one of the predictors is a statistically significant predictor of total 24-month spending. Second, we look at the card variable's 95% confidence interval.
```{r}
confint (mlr.model, level = 0.95)
```

The interval is [108.97, 469.7108]. We are 95% confident that, holding number of 24month visits constant, the true average spending for customers with a store credit card is between \$108.97 and \$469.69 higher than for customers without the card. This interval does not contain zero and is positive, so we have strong evidence that the card has a statistically significant positive effect on spending.
In conclusion, this analysis confirms that having a private-label credit card will meaningfully increases the amount of money a customer spends at the retailer. It is obvious that customers who visit more frequent will spend more money, but our model proves that the credit card will give a financial boost beyond just getting more people in the store. It shows that essentially if two customers visit the store the exact same number of times over a two year period, that the customer with the card will on average spend about $290 more than the one without one. It suggests that having a card is profitable for a company, and important for the retailers sales. A big limitation of the analysis is that the small sample size held back on showing a clearer picture of the data. It was large enough for statistical significance, but a larger sample would provide a tighter confidence interval for the true dollar impact of the card. In addition this data is only one clothing retailer, so it cannot be generalized to other retailers, industries or for general credit card behavior. Finally, since this is an observational study, we cannot for sure claim that the card causes people to spend more. It is possible that customers who already plan to buy expensive items are the ones who choose to get the card for rewards.
